case_analysis.focal_point: Whether submitting a fraudulent Medicaid claim that accurately names a real patient constitutes “us[ing]” that patient’s “means of identification” “during and in relation to” fraud under the federal aggravated identity theft statute.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1028A(a)(1) (aggravated identity theft) (and its relationship to the underlying healthcare fraud offense).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Dubin argues that § 1028A targets identity theft—misappropriating another person’s identifying information to pass oneself off as them or otherwise make identity central to the fraud—not ordinary billing fraud where a real patient’s identifying information is merely incidentally included as part of a claim. He contends the Fifth Circuit’s expansive reading effectively turns routine fraud cases (like overstating services on a claim tied to a real patient) into aggravated identity theft, dramatically increasing punishment via § 1028A’s mandatory consecutive sentence and raising legality/vagueness concerns that should be addressed by a narrowing construction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the evidence was sufficient because Dubin submitted a Medicaid claim that invoked a specific patient’s entitlement to reimbursement for services that were not provided as billed, and doing so necessarily required “use” of that patient’s means of identification to carry out the fraud. On that view, the patient’s identifying information was not incidental: it was the mechanism by which the false claim was presented as payable, satisfying § 1028A(a)(1). The government also suggests petitioner may have forfeited certain arguments (potentially triggering plain-error review).
key_precedents: Carducci v. Regan, 714 F.2d 171 (D.C. Cir. 1983) (Scalia, J.)
Rollins v. Home Depot USA, Inc., 8 F.4th 393 (5th Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: The government’s best point remains that patient identifiers are a but-for necessity for Medicaid reimbursement and thus “facilitate” the fraud, but that reading would make § 1028A a near-automatic mandatory add-on to routine billing fraud and leave “during and in relation to” with no real narrowing function. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith’s “purpose or effect” requirement helps draw the minimal, administrable line: the identifier must operate as an instrument of what makes the conduct wrongful (misrepresenting who is involved or entitled), not merely appear as accurate routing information in a claim fraudulent for other reasons. Justice Thomas’s ordinary-meaning concern underscores that “uses” connotes employing the identifier as a tool, and Flores-Figueroa’s identity-theft-centered framing makes it unlikely Congress meant to trigger a mandatory consecutive term where no one’s identity is exploited or misrepresented. A narrow holding on these facts preserves proportionality and institutional legitimacy while leaving room for § 1028A where identity misuse is integral to the fraud.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The government’s best point remains that a Medicaid claim cannot be processed without the patient’s identifier, so the name is a but-for facilitator of the fraud. But under the ordinary public meaning of “uses … a means of identification … during and in relation to,” the identifier must be employed as an instrumentality of what makes the conduct criminal, not merely included as accurate, routinized information that any claim must contain; otherwise the limiting phrase does no real narrowing work and § 1028A becomes a mandatory add-on to vast swaths of ordinary billing fraud. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith’s “purpose or effect” formulation strengthens that textual point by confirming a non-incidental nexus requirement, and Flores-Figueroa’s mens rea emphasis reinforces that Congress was targeting identity-centered misuse rather than truthful identifiers accompanying a lie about services. No colleague’s argument undermines that originalist reading of “use” and the relational phrase, so I would reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The government’s best point—that a Medicaid claim cannot be paid without the patient identifier—shows but-for relevance, but it does not establish that the defendant “used” the identifier as an instrument of the fraud as opposed to supplying accurate, administrative routing information. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor rightly invoke Smith’s “purpose or effect” gloss on identical “during and in relation to” language; here the purpose/effect of the identifier is to identify the real patient, not to make the misrepresentation about services/code/provider qualifications succeed in the way § 1028A targets. Justice Barrett’s ordinary-meaning point is also persuasive under a textualist approach: “uses a means of identification” connotes employing identity to deceive about who someone is or what they’re entitled to, not merely completing mandatory claim fields. Given Flores-Figueroa’s identity-theft framing and the severe mandatory consecutive penalty, I see no clear textual basis to transform routine overbilling into aggravated identity theft whenever a real name appears.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest likely argument for the government is that the patient’s identifiers were necessary to get Medicaid to pay, so the defendant “used” them “during and in relation to” the fraud; but under Smith’s “purpose or effect” test, necessity alone cannot erase the statute’s limiting function when the identifiers are accurate and merely administrative rather than identity-exploiting. Justice Kagan’s point about workability and coherence is persuasive: treating routine, accurate identifiers in billing as aggravated identity theft would make § 1028A a near-automatic add-on in healthcare fraud, producing disproportionate mandatory consecutive punishment and incentivizing overcharging that will fall hardest on low-level defendants. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity reminder also matters here because the government’s reading would dramatically expand a federal criminal statute with severe sentencing consequences absent clear textual direction. Nothing in Flores-Figueroa’s mens rea requirement suggests Congress meant to sweep in ordinary overbilling where the fraud is about the service rendered, not who the patient is.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s necessity/facilitation argument—that Medicaid can’t process a claim without a patient identifier—proves too much, because it would satisfy “uses … during and in relation to” whenever a required field is accurately supplied, leaving that limiting language with no real narrowing work. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith’s “purpose or effect” formulation best preserves statutory coherence: the identifier must be employed as an instrument of the deception about who is involved or entitled, not merely as truthful routing information accompanying a lie about services or codes. Flores-Figueroa, as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas note, reinforces that § 1028A is calibrated to identity-centered misuse, making it implausible Congress meant an automatic consecutive add-on for routine overbilling that happens to contain a real person’s name. On these facts the identity is accurate and incidental to the fraud’s crux, so the nexus required by the text is not met.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s best point remains but-for necessity: a Medicaid claim typically cannot be processed without a patient identifier, so the identifier “facilitates” payment and thus the fraud. But as Justice Sotomayor (invoking Smith) and the Chief Justice emphasize, “during and in relation to” requires a non-incidental nexus—purpose or effect—so the identifier must operate as an instrument of the deception, not merely appear as accurate, administratively required information while the falsity lies elsewhere (services, coding, provider qualifications). Justice Barrett’s ordinary-meaning point reinforces that “uses … a means of identification” naturally connotes employing identity to misrepresent who is involved or entitled, and Flores-Figueroa’s mens rea-sensitive reading cautions against converting § 1028A’s severe mandatory consecutive penalty into an automatic add-on for routine billing fraud. On a textualist/originalist reading—plus lenity if any real doubt persists—the statute is best confined to identity-centered misuse rather than incidental inclusion of a real person’s identifying data.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The government’s best contention remains the but-for necessity point: a Medicaid claim cannot be paid without the patient identifier, so the identifier “facilitates” the fraud. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, importing that theory into § 1028A effectively nullifies “during and in relation to” and converts the statute into a near-automatic consecutive add-on for routine overbilling whenever a real name appears—an outcome hard to reconcile with Congress’s calibrated, severe penalty and the identity-theft focus reflected in Flores-Figueroa. Justice Barrett’s ordinary-meaning point reinforces that “uses” in this context connotes employing the identifier as an instrument of deception (about who is involved/entitled), not merely providing accurate administrative information required to route a claim. Smith’s “purpose or effect” nexus, as Roberts and Sotomayor frame it, supplies a workable limiting principle that preserves proportionality and institutional legitimacy without rewriting the statute.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The government’s best argument—that a claim cannot be processed without a real patient identifier and so the defendant necessarily “used” it “during and in relation to” the fraud—still proves too much: it would convert § 1028A into an automatic, mandatory consecutive add-on for routine healthcare fraud whenever accurate identifiers appear, leaving the limiting phrase with little narrowing work. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith’s “purpose or effect” nexus is persuasive as a textual constraint: the identifier must be employed as an instrumentality of the deception, not merely as accurate routing information incidental to a lie about services or codes. Flores-Figueroa’s identity-centered framing, highlighted by Justices Thomas and Alito, reinforces that Congress aimed at misuse of identity as such, and nothing in the text clearly authorizes the sweeping expansion the government proposes given the severe mandatory penalty. Under an original public meaning approach attentive to statutory context and consequences that signal overbreadth, I remain with Petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s best point remains that the patient identifier is a but-for prerequisite to claim submission and thus “facilitates” payment, but that collapses § 1028A’s “during and in relation to” into mere administrative necessity and turns the statute into an automatic sentencing add-on for routine healthcare fraud. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith’s “purpose or effect” nexus persuasively cabins the statute to situations where identity information is an instrument of the deceit—about who is involved, entitled, or authorized—rather than accurate routing information accompanying a different misrepresentation about services or codes. Flores-Figueroa’s insistence that § 1028A’s elements do real work reinforces that Congress was targeting identity-theft-type misuse, and the severe mandatory consecutive penalty heightens the need for a clear, workable limiting principle. On pragmatic and fairness grounds, sweeping in truthful identifiers incidental to upcoding would create disproportionate consequences untethered to aggravated identity theft.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires that the defendant "use" another person’s "means of identification" "during and in relation to" the predicate offense, and that relational language, as construed in Smith v. United States, demands the identification have a purpose or effect with respect to the fraud—more than accident or coincidence. A narrow reading preserves the statute’s focus on aggravated identity theft rather than converting routine billing overstatements that happen to include accurate patient identifiers into a mandatory consecutive felony, which would risk overbreadth and undermine proportionality and institutional legitimacy. Here, where the patient’s identity was accurate and served only to locate the claim in Medicaid’s system, the gravamen of the fraud was the misrepresentation about services, not a misuse of identity. Consistent with judicial minimalism and respect for Congress’s calibration of penalties, the conviction should be vacated under a limiting construction of "uses ... during and in relation to" in § 1028A(a)(1).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1028A(a)(1) punishes one who “knowingly … uses, without lawful authority, a means of identification of another person” “during and in relation to” an enumerated felony; in ordinary public meaning, “uses” a means of identification connotes employing the identifier as an instrumentality of the crime, not merely including accurate identifying information as an incidental feature of a fraudulent claim. Reading “uses … during and in relation to” to cover any fraud that happens to contain a real patient’s name would collapse § 1028A into a sweeping sentencing add-on for routine billing fraud and disregard the limiting function of the statute’s operative verbs (“transfers, possesses, or uses”) and relation requirement. Flores-Figueroa v. United States (2009) confirms that § 1028A is keyed to identity-based wrongdoing by requiring knowledge that the means of identification belongs to “another person,” a mens rea that makes most sense where the identifier is being exploited as such rather than simply reported accurately in paperwork. Because Dubin did not misappropriate the patient’s identity or deploy the identifier to pretend to be someone else, the aggravated-identity-theft enhancement is not supported by the statute’s text as originally understood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) punishes “aggravated identity theft,” and its text—“knowingly transfers, possesses, or uses, without lawful authority, a means of identification of another person”—read in context with the statute’s title and the “during and in relation to” limitation, targets misuse of another’s identity as a thing, not every fraud that happens to include a real person’s identifying information. Treating routine Medicaid upcoding that correctly lists a real patient as “use” of that patient’s identification would collapse the distinction between ordinary fraud and identity theft, producing sweeping, mandatory consecutive punishment untethered to the statute’s ordinary meaning and practical design. Flores-Figueroa reinforces that § 1028A should be construed with attention to “identity theft” as the core concept, including reliance on the statute’s title as a legitimate interpretive aid, and counsels against expansive readings that turn incidental identifiers into aggravated identity theft. Because the patient’s name here served a billing-administrative function rather than a misappropriation of identity to perpetrate the fraud, § 1028A(a)(1) is not satisfied.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires that a defendant "use" another person’s "means of identification" "during and in relation to" the predicate fraud, which—under this Court’s interpretation of identical "in relation to" language—demands a non-coincidental nexus that at least facilitates the underlying crime. Smith v. United States, 508 U.S. 223, 237–38 (1993), makes clear the connection must have some "purpose or effect" and not be merely incidental; here, the gravamen of the Medicaid fraud is the misrepresentation about services rendered, not a misrepresentation about the patient’s identity. Reading § 1028A to cover any fraudulent claim that includes a real patient’s accurate identifying information would transform routine billing fraud into aggravated identity theft and trigger a mandatory consecutive sentence in a way that is disproportionate and invites overcharging, harming vulnerable defendants and distorting access to justice. A narrower construction—limiting § 1028A to cases where identity misuse is central to the fraud (e.g., impersonation or misrepresentation of who is entitled)—best fits the statutory text and avoids sweeping ordinary fraud into a harsh mandatory regime.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires that the defendant “use[] … a means of identification of another person” “during and in relation to” the predicate fraud, which is best read to cover situations where the identifier is itself the instrumentality that makes the conduct identity-theft-like, not where a real patient’s name is merely a routine attribute of a billing claim. A broad construction would make § 1028A a near-automatic add-on in ordinary healthcare overbilling cases—an unworkable, incoherent result given Congress’s targeted focus on “identity theft” and the statute’s mandatory consecutive penalty. Consistent with Flores-Figueroa’s insistence on giving meaningful content to § 1028A’s limiting terms, the “use … during and in relation to” language should be construed to require more than incidental inclusion of accurate patient identifying information in an otherwise fraudulent claim. On these facts, Dubin’s fraud was about the nature and amount of services billed, not misappropriating the patient’s identity in a way that § 1028A was designed to punish.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) imposes a mandatory consecutive penalty only when the defendant "knowingly ... uses, without lawful authority, a means of identification of another person" "during and in relation to" the predicate fraud; read in context and consistent with ordinary meaning, that requires the identification to play a genuine, operative role in the criminality—not merely appear as an accurate, incidental descriptor on a claim otherwise fraudulent as to services or billing codes. A contrary reading would collapse § 1028A into a sweeping enhancement for commonplace billing fraud whenever a real patient’s name is included, a construction that strains the statutory phrase "during and in relation to" and creates serious overbreadth concerns best avoided by a narrowing reading, especially given the statute’s mandatory consecutive sentence. Flores-Figueroa v. United States underscores that § 1028A must be read with care and precision, resisting expansive interpretations that transform it into a general-purpose sentencing add-on untethered from identity theft as such. Where the statute’s reach is at least doubtful on these facts, the rule of lenity counsels against the government’s broader construction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires that the defendant "use" another person’s means of identification "during and in relation to" the predicate fraud, and that limiting phrase must do real work to ensure a meaningful nexus rather than sweeping in routine overbilling that happens to include accurate patient identifiers. As in Smith v. United States (interpreting identical "during and in relation to" language in § 924(c)), the identifying information must have some purpose or effect with respect to the predicate offense and not be merely coincidental or incidental to the billing fraud. Reading § 1028A to cover any fraudulent claim that contains a real patient’s name would dramatically expand the statute beyond the identity-theft problem Congress targeted, create serious workability and line-drawing concerns, and risk converting ordinary healthcare-fraud prosecutions into mandatory consecutive two-year identity-theft cases without a clear historical or traditional fit. Respect for precedent, statutory structure, and practical administrability therefore favors a narrower construction under which Dubin’s conduct is standard billing fraud but not aggravated identity theft absent a misappropriation or identity-centered use of the identifier.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, § 1028A(a)(1) requires that the defendant “knowingly … uses, without lawful authority, a means of identification of another person” “during and in relation to” the predicate felony; in ordinary usage, “use” in this context connotes employing another’s identifying information as a means of misrepresentation about who is involved, not merely including accurate identifiers as a routine feature of a billing submission. Reading “uses … during and in relation to” to cover any fraudulent claim that contains a real patient’s name would risk collapsing the statute into a sweeping add-on for ordinary fraud, undermining the limiting work of “during and in relation to” and producing a mandatory consecutive penalty untethered to identity-centered wrongdoing. Flores-Figueroa v. United States, 556 U.S. 646 (2009), reinforces that § 1028A targets the wrongful use of another person’s identification as such (and requires knowledge it belongs to another), supporting a narrower construction where the identity misuse is integral to the fraud rather than incidental. Respect for precedent counsels against adopting the Fifth Circuit’s expansive approach absent clearer statutory text, especially given the significant sentencing consequences of § 1028A’s mandatory two-year consecutive term.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) is best read to require that the defendant’s “use” of another person’s “means of identification” be at the crux of what makes the conduct fraudulent—i.e., an identity-theft-type misuse—rather than the merely incidental inclusion of accurate patient identifiers in routine billing fraud. A broader reading would give the statute a “breathtaking” reach, converting many garden-variety fraud cases into aggravated identity theft and triggering a mandatory consecutive two-year sentence, a practical consequence that counsels a narrowing construction consistent with procedural fairness. This Court has repeatedly cautioned against expansive interpretations of federal criminal statutes when a narrower, textually plausible construction is available, and that interpretive discipline supports limiting § 1028A to situations where the identity information is used to misrepresent who is involved in the transaction. Accordingly, submitting a fraudulent Medicaid claim that correctly names a real patient, without more, should not satisfy the “uses … during and in relation to” element of § 1028A(a)(1).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether submitting a Medicaid claim that includes a real patient’s identifying information, but falsely overstates the services provided, constitutes “us[ing]” that person’s “means of identification” “during and in relation to” healthcare fraud under the federal aggravated identity theft statute.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1028A(a)(1) (aggravated identity theft) (as applied in connection with healthcare fraud predicates).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Dubin argues that § 1028A is aimed at true identity theft—misappropriating someone’s identity (e.g., impersonation or passing oneself off as another)—and should not apply whenever a defendant commits fraud in a way that incidentally includes accurate identifying information (like a patient name/Medicaid ID) in a billing submission. He contends that treating routine billing details as aggravated identity theft would dramatically expand § 1028A to cover a wide range of ordinary fraud cases, effectively adding a mandatory consecutive two-year sentence whenever any identifier is used in the paperwork, even if the identifier is not the “crux” of the deception. Petitioner-oriented amici further suggest that a narrower construction is required to avoid overbreadth and vagueness problems and to preserve the separation of powers/legality concerns that arise when a vague standard permits prosecutors to convert many frauds into aggravated identity theft.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that the jury had sufficient evidence to find that Dubin “use[d]” a real patient’s “means of identification” to commit fraud because the Medicaid claim invoked a specific patient’s entitlement to reimbursement for services allegedly provided to that patient, and the claim was false as to the nature/extent of the service (e.g., a fictitious three-hour licensed-psychologist exam). In the government’s view, using the patient’s identifiers was not incidental—it was the mechanism by which Dubin sought payment—and thus falls within the ordinary meaning of “use” under § 1028A(a)(1). The government also suggests there may be appellate-forfeiture/standard-of-review constraints on petitioner’s narrower “use” theory.
key_precedents: Rollins v. Home Depot USA, Inc., 8 F.4th 393 (5th Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to stress that the claim form cannot be processed without the patient identifiers, but treating that necessary “routing” function as sufficient would make § 1028A a virtually automatic consecutive add-on to § 1347 whenever accurate identifiers are required—a result hard to square with Congress’s use of the limiting phrase “during and in relation to” in a mandatory-minimum statute. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on our “in relation to” cases (including Smith) reinforces that the identifier must have a non-incidental nexus to what makes the conduct deceptive or meaningfully facilitates the fraud beyond mere presence on paperwork. Flores-Figueroa, as Justice Kagan and others note, counsels careful, element-focused narrowing where severe penalties are at stake; it does not impose an “impersonation-only” rule, but it supports reading “uses … during and in relation to” to require identity misuse that is central to the fraud’s deceit. On that narrower ground, truthful identifiers that merely enable claim submission are not enough when the misrepresentation concerns only the services billed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that the patient identifiers are a necessary mechanism for reimbursement and thus are “used … during and in relation to” the fraud—fails at the level of ordinary public meaning in context because it reduces the limiting phrase to a mere but-for test and effectively makes § 1028A an automatic add-on whenever a form requires truthful identifiers. Chief Justice Roberts’s overbreadth concern is not a policy override but a textual coherence point: reading “uses … during and in relation to” to cover routine, accurate routing information deprives those words of any narrowing function in a mandatory consecutive-penalty statute. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on our “in relation to” cases (including Smith) supports the better textual boundary: the identifier must be employed as an instrumentality of what makes the representation deceptive, not merely included while the lie concerns only the services billed. Flores-Figueroa’s insistence on careful, element-by-element reading of § 1028A’s severe penalty reinforces that we should not expand “use” beyond its aggravated identity-theft sense absent clearer text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s overbreadth point seriously: if “during and in relation to” is read too loosely, § 1028A could become a frequent add-on in billing-fraud prosecutions. But that practical concern cannot justify rewriting the statute’s operative words—here the defendant “uses” a real patient’s “means of identification” as the mechanism by which the false claim is submitted and paid, and that use plainly occurs “during and in relation to” the § 1347 fraud because the identifiers are what connect the fabricated service to a reimbursable beneficiary. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith does not move me; Smith requires a real nexus, and the identifiers are not coincidental—they facilitate the fraud by enabling payment through the program’s identity-based routing. Flores-Figueroa dealt with scienter (knowing the identifier belongs to another person), and I do not read it to impose an extra-textual “impersonation-only” limitation on “uses” or to narrow the statute merely because the penalty is severe.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest textual argument—that the claim “uses” the patient’s identifiers as the mechanism for reimbursement—still reads “during and in relation to” down to a but-for formality and makes § 1028A a near-automatic add-on in routine billing fraud, which is hard to square with a mandatory consecutive penalty absent a clearer congressional command. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain that our “in relation to” cases (including Smith) require a meaningful nexus: the identifier must do real work in the deception, not merely appear as accurate routing information while the lie concerns what service was provided. Flores-Figueroa, though about scienter, reinforces a cautionary approach to expanding § 1028A beyond aggravated identity misuse, supporting a limiting construction that preserves fair notice and avoids disproportionate sentencing leverage. On these facts, the fraud turned on the services billed, not who the patient was, so the identifiers were incidental rather than the instrumentality of the deceit.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that the identifiers are a factual mechanism for getting a fraudulent claim paid, but that reading effectively reduces “during and in relation to” to a but-for test and turns § 1028A into an automatic add-on whenever a form requires accurate identifying fields. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, our “in relation to” cases (including Smith) demand a limiting nexus: the means of identification must do real work in what makes the conduct fraudulent, not merely appear as truthful routing information while the misrepresentation concerns the service or amount. Flores-Figueroa, while addressing scienter, still reinforces the need to read § 1028A’s elements with care given its severe mandatory consecutive penalty—counseling against the government’s expansive construction absent clearer textual command. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, Petitioners’ interpretation preserves statutory coherence and workable administrability by keeping § 1028A focused on identity misuse central to the deception rather than ubiquitous paperwork.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that the patient identifiers are a factual but-for prerequisite to getting Medicaid to pay, and in that sense they are “used” in submitting the claim. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, reading “uses … during and in relation to” to cover any truthful, required identifier on a form would drain those limiting words of independent work and effectively convert § 1028A into an automatic mandatory add-on for routine billing fraud—an expansion the text does not clearly command. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Smith underscores that “in relation to” requires a real nexus to what makes the conduct wrongful; here the deception is about the service and amount, not who the beneficiary is, so the identifier functions as accurate routing information rather than the instrument of the fraud. Flores-Figueroa’s careful, element-by-element approach to § 1028A’s severe consecutive penalty reinforces that we should not broaden “use” by abstraction, and any remaining uncertainty should be resolved by lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that the patient identifiers are a factual “but-for” prerequisite to submitting a Medicaid claim, but that reading effectively drains “during and in relation to” of any limiting function and risks turning § 1028A into an automatic mandatory consecutive enhancement for ordinary billing fraud. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about preserving a meaningful boundary is consistent with our “in relation to” cases (as Justice Sotomayor notes via Smith), which require more than mere presence on the paperwork—there must be a non-incidental nexus to what makes the conduct wrongful. Flores-Figueroa’s cautionary approach to § 1028A’s severe penalty supports resisting an interpretation that expands the statute by implication whenever accurate identifiers appear on required forms. Here, the deceit was about what services were rendered and billed, not who received them, so the identifiers functioned as truthful routing information rather than the instrumentality of deception.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s contention that the patient identifiers are the “necessary mechanism” for reimbursement is the best argument for the government, but on the ordinary meaning of “uses … a means of identification … during and in relation to” the predicate, the identifier must do more than serve as accurate routing information—it must be employed as an instrumentality that makes the conduct deceptive in a relevant way. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s points about preserving limiting work for “in relation to,” consistent with Smith, sharpen that textual constraint: a mere but-for role would collapse § 1028A into a mandatory add-on whenever a form requires a name or number, an implausible construction for a severe consecutive penalty. Justice Thomas is also right that context (including the statute’s focus on aggravated identity theft, as reflected in Flores-Figueroa’s careful element-by-element reading) counsels against expanding “use” to cover truthful identifiers where the fraud concerns only the services billed. Because Alito’s reading relies on abstraction that erases the statute’s narrowing phrases, it does not undermine my originalist/textualist view that § 1028A targets identity misuse central to the deception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s textual point—that identifiers are the mechanism by which a Medicaid claim gets paid—cannot, by itself, satisfy § 1028A’s requirement that the defendant “use” the means of identification “during and in relation to” the predicate, because that would make the enhancement effectively automatic whenever a form includes truthful identifiers, leaving the limiting nexus language with no real work to do. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on our “in relation to” jurisprudence (including Smith) is persuasive here: the identifier must have a meaningful connection to what makes the claim fraudulent, not mere temporal overlap or routine routing information when the deception concerns the service provided. Flores-Figueroa, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan note, counsels caution in expanding a mandatory consecutive penalty without a clear narrowing principle in the statutory elements; that interpretive discipline supports reading “use” as identity misuse central to the fraud rather than accurate identification incidental to billing. Even if the government’s broader reading is plausible in the abstract, the combination of statutory coherence and lenity in a severe penal scheme keeps me with Petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) should be read narrowly to preserve Congress’s targeted aim at aggravated identity theft and to avoid converting routine fraud cases into automatic two-year consecutive penalties whenever accurate identifying information appears in required paperwork. Treating any inclusion of a real patient’s identifiers on a Medicaid claim as “us[ing]” a “means of identification” “during and in relation to” fraud risks a sweeping, “breathtaking” expansion of federal criminal liability that a narrower, reasonable construction can avoid, consistent with the narrow-construction approach in ambiguous criminal statutes. A limiting construction best protects institutional legitimacy by keeping § 1028A tied to identity-misuse that is central to the fraud, rather than merely incidental compliance information in billing. That approach also avoids prosecutorial overreach concerns inherent in broad readings of mandatory consecutive sentencing statutes under § 1028A(b)(2).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1028A(a)(1) targets aggravated “identity theft,” and in its ordinary public meaning that phrase connotes misappropriating another’s identity—using an identifier to pass oneself off as someone else or otherwise to take on that person’s identity—rather than merely including accurate patient identifiers in routine billing while lying about the services. Reading “uses … a means of identification … during and in relation to” to cover any fraud that happens to contain a name or Medicaid number would transform § 1028A into a general sentencing enhancement for paperwork fraud, untethered from the statute’s identity-theft focus, and it is not this Court’s role to expand criminal liability beyond the statute’s original meaning. Flores-Figueroa v. United States underscores that § 1028A must be interpreted with attention to its ordinary meaning and its title (“Aggravated Identity Theft”), and that the statute is not a catchall for every fraudulent act involving identifying information. Because Dubin’s deception concerned the nature and amount of services rendered, not the patient’s identity, the identifiers were incidental to the billing mechanism and do not constitute the kind of “use” § 1028A criminalizes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) applies when a defendant "knowingly transfers, possesses, or uses" a "means of identification of another person" "during and in relation to" a predicate offense, and a Medicaid claim necessarily uses the patient’s identifying information as the vehicle to invoke that patient’s entitlement to reimbursement. Here, the misrepresentation about the service provided was effectuated through the claim tied to a specific individual’s identifiers, so the use was not merely incidental paperwork but integral to committing health care fraud under § 1347. Flores-Figueroa v. United States confirms that § 1028A requires knowledge that the identifier belongs to a real person, but it does not narrow the ordinary meaning of “use” to only impersonation-type scenarios. Reading “use” narrowly to exclude fraudulent billing would create an atextual carveout and undermine Congress’s evident purpose to add a mandatory consecutive penalty when real persons’ identifiers are employed to facilitate enumerated frauds.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires not merely that an identifier appear in paperwork, but that the defendant “use[]” another’s “means of identification” “during and in relation to” the predicate fraud—i.e., in a way that at least facilitates the fraud and is more than coincidental. Under this Court’s construction of “in relation to” in Smith v. United States, the identity use must be integral to what makes the conduct criminal; treating routine inclusion of accurate patient identifiers on a Medicaid claim as aggravated identity theft would dramatically and unfairly expand § 1028A and add a mandatory consecutive two-year term to a wide swath of ordinary fraud cases. A narrower reading better reflects Congress’s evident focus on true identity theft/misappropriation and avoids giving prosecutors sweeping leverage that can distort charging and sentencing, with especially harsh consequences for defendants in the criminal system. Because Dubin’s deception concerned the services billed, not an identity misappropriation, the patient’s identifying information was incidental to the fraud and does not satisfy § 1028A’s limiting “during and in relation to” requirement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) punishes “us[ing]” another’s “means of identification” “during and in relation to” a predicate fraud, but that language is best read to require that the identifier itself play a meaningful role in the fraudulent conduct—i.e., the misuse of identity is at the crux of what makes the transaction deceptive, not merely a routine feature of billing paperwork. Reading “use” to cover any healthcare-fraud claim that contains accurate patient identifiers would effectively add a mandatory consecutive two-year sentence to a broad swath of ordinary overbilling cases, a result in tension with statutory coherence and workability given § 1028A’s targeted design as an aggravated, identity-centered enhancement. Flores-Figueroa v. United States underscores that § 1028A is not a limitless add-on: the Court insisted on a narrowing scienter requirement to prevent overexpansion of the statute’s severe mandatory penalty, and a similarly careful construction of “use … during and in relation to” is warranted here. Because the fraud alleged is overstatement of services rather than misrepresentation about who received them, the patient identifier is best treated as incidental to the deception and outside § 1028A’s core.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires that a defendant “use[]” another’s “means of identification” “during and in relation to” the predicate fraud; read in ordinary terms, that targets cases where the identifier itself is employed as an instrumentality of the deception (e.g., misrepresenting who received services), not where accurate identifiers merely appear in paperwork while the lie concerns the services rendered. The government’s broader construction would effectively append a mandatory consecutive two-year sentence to vast swaths of garden-variety healthcare fraud whenever a claim necessarily includes a patient’s name or Medicaid number, a sweeping expansion that Congress did not clearly command in the text. Where the statute plausibly bears both readings and the broader reading carries “cascading” penal consequences, the rule of lenity counsels adopting the narrower construction. See United States v. Santos, 553 U.S. 507, 514 (2008).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Text, structure, and history suggest § 1028A(a)(1) targets misuse of another’s identity as an instrument of the fraud, not the mere inclusion of accurate identifying information that is ancillary to a billing overstatement; reading “uses … during and in relation to” to cover routine claims risks turning § 1028A into a near-automatic two-year add-on for many healthcare frauds, an impractical and overbroad result Congress is unlikely to have intended. A limiting construction also better respects precedent and traditional rule-of-law concerns about fair notice and prosecutorial discretion, consistent with the Court’s approach to narrowing readings of broad criminal statutes (cf. Flores-Figueroa v. United States and the ordinary understanding of “identity theft”). Applying “use” only where the means of identification is at the crux of what makes the conduct fraudulent preserves workability and avoids collapsing § 1028A into the predicate offense itself. Under that reading, submitting a claim that truthfully identifies a real patient but lies about the service provided is healthcare fraud, but not necessarily aggravated identity theft absent identity misuse akin to impersonation or misappropriation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) requires that the defendant "use" another person’s "means of identification" "during and in relation to" the predicate fraud, and the ordinary public meaning of that phrase—read in context—demands more than the incidental inclusion of accurate identifying information in a billing form. As in Flores-Figueroa v. United States, 556 U.S. 646 (2009), we construe § 1028A’s elements with close attention to ordinary usage and the statute’s targeted aim at identity theft; otherwise the government’s reading would convert a vast range of routine frauds involving paperwork identifiers into mandatory consecutive two-year enhancements. A narrower construction also better respects methodological consistency and avoids the serious overbreadth/line-drawing concerns that arise when prosecutors can attach § 1028A whenever any identifier appears in a claim, and any remaining ambiguity is resolved by the rule of lenity. Because Dubin’s deception concerned the nature and extent of services, not who the patient was, the patient’s identifiers were not “used” in the aggravated-identity-theft sense required by § 1028A.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1028A(a)(1) targets aggravated identity theft, and its “during and in relation to” requirement is best read to cover situations where the misuse of another’s “means of identification” is itself a genuine component of the fraud—rather than merely accurate, routine billing information attached to a claim that is false in other respects. Reading “use” to encompass any claim that includes a real patient’s identifiers would convert a wide range of ordinary healthcare-fraud prosecutions into mandatory consecutive two-year identity-theft offenses, an overexpansion with serious sentencing consequences and uneven enforcement risks. Where the text plausibly supports both a narrow and a broad construction, the rule of lenity counsels adopting the narrower, defendant-favorable reading. See 18 U.S.C. § 1028A(a)(1); United States v. Santos, 553 U.S. 507, 514 (2008).
